lessons.title: Map reading: scale, grid references, contours and gradient

objectives: Calculate distances from a map scale
Give four- and six-figure grid references and bearings
reviewNotes: The contour figure is schematic and not to scale.
Confirm how many digits the syllabus expects in grid references and whether bearings use grid north.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Scale and distance
blocks.md: A scale such as **1:50 000** means 1 cm on the map is 50 000 cm (0.5 km) on the ground. Distance = map length × scale denominator, then convert units: 100 000 cm = 1 km. A straight line is easy; for a curved road lay string along it and measure the string.

blocks.title: Grid references and bearings
blocks.md: Give **eastings first** (along the corridor) then **northings** (up the stairs). A four-figure reference names a grid square; a six-figure reference adds tenths for precision. A **bearing** is measured clockwise from grid north, with three digits (e.g. 045° is north-east).

blocks.caption: Concentric contours show a hill.
blocks.alt: Three concentric rings labelled 100, 200 and 300 metres around a hilltop.

blocks.title: Contours and gradient
blocks.md: **Contours** join points of equal height. Close together means steep; far apart means gentle; closed rings are hills or summits. **Gradient** = vertical interval ÷ horizontal distance, often written 1 in n. Convert both to the same unit first.

blocks.title: Frequent mistakes
blocks.md:
- Reading northings before eastings.
- Forgetting to convert cm to km.
- Mixing up height difference and distance in the gradient fraction.
- Taking bearings anticlockwise or from magnetic north.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Distance
blocks.statement: Two villages are 6.4 cm apart on a map of scale 1:50 000. Find the real distance in km.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Gradient
blocks.statement: A road climbs from 400 m to 500 m over a horizontal distance of 2 km. Find the gradient as 1 in n.

lessons.title: Statistics, GIS, remote sensing and fieldwork

objectives: Calculate mean, median, mode and range and interpret scatter graphs
Explain what GIS and remote sensing are used for
Plan a fieldwork enquiry with suitable sampling
reviewNotes: Check whether the syllabus requires Spearman’s rank correlation and standard deviation (not covered here).
All data in this lesson are invented for practice.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Averages and spread
blocks.md: **Mean** = sum ÷ number of values. **Median** = middle value of the ordered list. **Mode** = most frequent value. **Range** = largest − smallest. A scatter graph shows the relationship between two variables: points rising from left to right show **positive correlation**, falling points **negative correlation**, and no pattern means none. Correlation does not prove cause.

blocks.title: GIS and remote sensing
blocks.md: A **GIS** (geographic information system) stores data in **layers** (roads, rivers, population, land use) that can be overlaid and analysed. **Remote sensing** uses satellites and aircraft to record the Earth’s surface, for example to monitor forest loss, floods, crop condition and urban growth. GPS gives positions.

blocks.caption: A scatter graph showing positive correlation (illustrative data).
blocks.alt: Scatter graph with points rising from bottom-left to top-right.

blocks.title: Fieldwork steps
blocks.md: 1. Choose a question and hypothesis. 2. Plan methods, equipment and safety. 3. Choose a **sampling** method: random, systematic (every nth) or stratified (proportional groups). 4. Collect data. 5. Present with graphs and maps. 6. Analyse, conclude and evaluate (reliability, bias, limits).

blocks.title: Pitfalls
blocks.md:
- The median needs the data sorted first.
- For an even number of values the median is the mean of the two middle values.
- A small sample may be unreliable.
- Do not claim that correlation proves one factor causes the other.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Averages
blocks.statement: Monthly rainfall (illustrative, mm): 10, 25, 25, 40, 50. Find mean, median, mode and range.
blocks.answer: Mean 30 mm, median 25 mm, mode 25 mm, range 40 mm.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Sampling
blocks.statement: A student wants to study the opinions of 200 market traders: 120 sell food, 80 sell cloth. She will sample 20. How many from each group in a stratified sample?
